segments.title: Designing a 1926 all-forward fast battleship
segments.body: The build begins with a 1926 British battleship of about 50,000 tons and a minimum speed of 28 knots. Geared turbines and an auxiliary diesel support that speed, while anti-torpedo protection, a double hull, and the initial armour scheme consume much of the displacement. Three quadruple 16-inch turrets sit forward and can bring all twelve guns onto a target ahead. The arrangement is openly playful rather than a plausible historical proposal, but the game makes the competing demands of firepower, speed, protection, internal volume, and firing arcs easy to follow.

evidence.note: He sets the speed and displacement, chooses machinery and protection, and builds an explicitly playful all-forward twelve-gun design.

segments.summary: An Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts build explores how speed, protection, machinery, and twelve 16-inch guns compete for space and displacement.

segments.title: Cutting weight without abandoning the battleship concept
segments.body: The experimental battleship initially comes in roughly 6,000 tons overweight, making every design preference compete for the remaining displacement. The build reduces range, changes the barbette arrangement, adopts all-or-nothing armour, and relaxes bulkhead protection until the design fits. When a little capacity remains, it goes to four-inch secondary guns and small increases in deck and belt armour. The running total makes the cumulative cost of weapons, machinery, protection, and hull performance visible. A paper specification cannot carry every desirable feature.

evidence.note: He removes thousands of tons through range, barbette, bulkhead, and armour choices, then allocates the margin to secondary guns and protection.

segments.summary: A 6,000-ton excess forces visible compromises in range, bulkheads, barbettes, armour distribution, and secondary weapons.

segments.title: Building an explicitly ahistorical Spanish opponent
segments.body: The Spanish side receives a large hull, 25-knot speed, oil firing, seasoned crews, anti-torpedo protection, and all-or-nothing armour. A conventional aft-turret arrangement makes the result look jokingly like a Spanish Iowa, while five-inch secondaries consume some of the remaining margin. The ship is explicitly fictional, and even its 25-knot speed exceeds what Spanish ships of the period actually achieved. Its capabilities belong to the game scenario rather than the historical Spanish Navy.

evidence.note: He constructs the Spanish opponent, labels it fictional, and contrasts the design with Spain's actual interwar capability.

segments.summary: The opposing design becomes a large, 25-knot Spanish battleship whose generous armament is separated clearly from historical Spanish capability.

segments.title: Writing treaty rules without inviting evasions
segments.body: Creative accounting is treated as an unavoidable feature of arms control rather than a surprise that can be legislated away. Excessive specificity gives governments and designers more boundaries to reinterpret, while broader restrictions leave fewer manufactured loopholes. The later London treaties tried to prevent evasion through detailed provisions and produced a different set of incentives. The practical choice is between broad limits that are easier to enforce and intricate rules that signatories can game.

evidence.note: He contrasts broad treaty rules with detailed provisions that invite creative accounting.

segments.summary: A question about creative accounting leads to the problem of making naval treaty rules enforceable.
segments.question: How could an equitable treaty work if participants used creative accounting?
segments.answerShort: No rule set eliminates evasion, but broad limits are less likely to manufacture loopholes than highly detailed restrictions.

segments.title: Capital-ship losses also destroy decades of experience
segments.body: A viewer contrasts the losses aboard Hood, Prince of Wales, and Repulse and totals more than two thousand sailors, including senior admirals and experienced captains. The people are the hardest part of a capital-ship loss to replace. A new ship can be built, but the accumulated professional experience of careers reaching roughly forty years cannot be recreated on the same schedule. Capital-ship attrition removes command knowledge and trained personnel along with tonnage.

evidence.note: A viewer lists the human losses from three British capital ships, and Dr. Clarke stresses that ships are easier to recreate than decades of personnel experience.

segments.summary: The loss of Hood, Prince of Wales, and Repulse is measured in irreplaceable professional experience as well as ships and casualties.
segments.question: What made the loss of Hood, Prince of Wales, and Repulse so costly beyond the ships themselves?
segments.answerShort: The crews were harder to replace than the hulls, especially senior officers whose professional experience had taken decades to build.

segments.title: Replacement cycles instead of preserving Hood
segments.body: Hood's original structure places a hard limit on modernization. Under the proposed system, she could remain among the last pre-treaty ships because she sat close to the new limits, but she would ultimately be replaced. A continuing construction cycle would let Britain learn from successive treaty battleship designs instead of waiting for one late generation such as the King George V class. Regular replacement preserves design experience and avoids placing the entire burden of modernization on ageing ships.

evidence.note: He explains Hood's design limits and an iterative replacement process.

segments.summary: The proposed treaty would encourage iterative replacement designs rather than keeping Hood and Repulse indefinitely.
segments.question: How would Britain make Hood, Repulse, and Prince of Wales as capable as possible under this treaty?
segments.answerShort: Hood would ultimately be replaced, while recurring construction would produce successive improved designs rather than one final treaty generation.

segments.title: Why battlecruisers do not make battleships obsolete
segments.body: Choosing an engagement is different from surviving in the battle line. A battlecruiser can use speed and manoeuvre to avoid a slower battleship, but that freedom does not erase the battleship's protection or firepower. If the battlecruiser accepts a direct fight, each hit is likely to hurt it more because it lacks equivalent armour. It therefore needs repeated success in positioning and damage avoidance, whereas the battleship can absorb mistakes more readily.

evidence.note: He explains the battlecruiser's speed advantage and vulnerability to hits.

segments.summary: Speed lets a battlecruiser avoid an unfavourable fight, but it cannot replace a battleship's protection.
segments.question: Would Hood make older American battleships obsolete?
segments.answerShort: No. A battlecruiser can avoid a battleship, but it does not have the protection to make battleships obsolete in a direct fight.

segments.title: Security as the basis of treaty stability
segments.body: Making every fleet weaker does not guarantee peace. Complete disarmament would have to be universal and credible. Otherwise, each state needs enough strength to believe it can defend itself. The United States and United Kingdom illustrate why those secure levels cannot be numerically identical. Durable ratios depend on political security rather than equal weakness.

evidence.note: He contrasts equal weakness with security sufficient for self-defence.

segments.summary: A treaty lasts only if its signatories feel able to defend themselves under it.
segments.question: Could an equitable naval treaty have guaranteed peace?
segments.answerShort: No treaty guarantees peace, but one is more durable when participants feel secure rather than permanently weakened.

segments.title: Do not write a treaty that requires lying
segments.body: A viewer recalls the advice never to give an order that will not be obeyed, and the same principle applies to treaty drafting. A nominal prohibition has little value when the agreement makes evasion or misreporting the expected response. Compliance must be plausible for the parties being regulated. Formal precision alone does not make an agreement enforceable.

evidence.note: He agrees with the maxim and applies it directly to treaty compliance.

segments.summary: A maxim about unenforceable orders becomes a compact rule for writing naval agreements that states can actually obey.
segments.question: Does the maxim 'never give an order that will not be obeyed' also apply to naval treaties?
segments.answerShort: Yes. A treaty should not be written in a way that automatically forces its signatories to lie.

segments.title: A flexible 3-3-2 British building programme
segments.body: A viewer proposes a recurring 3-3-2 Royal Navy battleship programme, with authority to add another hull when an external threat appears. The schedule would establish a core of fast battleships while retaining Hood and Renown long enough to test whether reconstruction could preserve a battlecruiser hedge. The comment also treats extra construction and modernization as employment measures during the Great Depression, linking fleet replacement to continuity of shipyard work. The video gives no substantive reply, so this remains the viewer's counterfactual rather than an endorsed programme.

evidence.note: A viewer proposes a flexible 3-3-2 battleship schedule, battlecruiser reconstruction, and added shipbuilding work during the Great Depression.

segments.summary: A viewer links recurring fast-battleship construction and battlecruiser reconstruction to threat response and Depression-era shipyard employment.

segments.title: The limits of rebuilding old capital ships
segments.body: New machinery cannot wholly overcome the internal arrangement of older ships such as Lion, Princess Royal, and Tiger. Each hull was laid out around the technology available when it was designed. A refit can adapt that arrangement only so far before the old design stops keeping pace with newer ships. Reconstruction may improve a capital ship without making it the equal of a clean-sheet design.

evidence.note: He explains why internal design constrains reconstruction.

segments.summary: Older hulls can be improved, but their internal arrangements limit how far modernization can keep pace.
segments.question: Would retaining and oil-converting older battlecruisers be better than keeping older battleships?
segments.answerShort: It could be interesting, but modernization cannot fully overcome an old hull's original internal and technological limits.

segments.title: Why fast battleships remove Hood's escape margin
segments.body: A viewer suggests that Hood's speed protected her until the fast-battleship generation arrived. Against slower battleships she could decline the action, but battle damage could reduce the speed margin she needed to escape. Fast battleships combine enough speed to pursue with armour built to remain in the fight. The transition therefore undermines the battlecruiser's defensive reliance on speed before it necessarily renders the ship mechanically useless.

evidence.note: He explains that damage could erase Hood's speed margin and that fast battleships combined pursuit speed with battle-line armour.

segments.summary: Hood's speed could avoid older battleships, but damage and the arrival of fast battleships made that defence increasingly fragile.
segments.question: Why did Hood's speed stop offering the same protection once fast battleships appeared?
segments.answerShort: Damage could take away Hood's ability to disengage, while fast battleships could keep up and survive return fire behind battleship armour.

segments.title: A 10:7 ratio and Japanese security
segments.body: The argument is that a 10:7 ratio would bind the larger British and American industrial bases more strongly than it binds Japan. Japanese leaders would still understand that they could not win an unrestricted building race, but the ratio would make the treaty feel protective rather than permanently humiliating. By contrast, 5:3 encourages continual demonstrations of strength because Japan starts from a position it regards as insecure. The intended effect is deterrence through sufficient security, rather than an illusion of equal war-winning power.

evidence.note: He compares the security effects of 10:7 and 5:3 ratios.

segments.summary: The proposed 10:7 ratio aims to bind larger fleets while avoiding Japan's sense of permanent inferiority.
segments.question: Why would the equitable treaty be less likely to collapse in the 1930s?
segments.answerShort: A 10:7 ratio could make Japan feel secure while still constraining the United States and Britain, unlike a ratio that made Japan feel permanently weak.

segments.title: Choosing a Washington baseline for the London treaties
segments.body: A question about refits, equivalent replacement, and definitions for smaller ships leads to a choice about the next stage of the treaty series. One route starts from the Washington Naval Treaty as negotiated and asks what a more equitable London settlement might have changed. The other treats the proposed equitable Washington settlement as the starting point and extends it into London. No choice is made here; the issue is deferred until the London treaty discussion.

evidence.note: He considers whether the later London discussion should begin from the historical Washington treaty or the equitable scenario proposed in this series.

segments.summary: The next counterfactual can begin from the historical Washington settlement or continue from the proposed equitable alternative.
segments.question: Would the London treaty follow the historical Washington system or the proposed equitable alternative?
segments.answerShort: The video leaves both starting points open and defers the choice to the later London treaty discussion.

segments.title: How national priorities shape treaty battleships
segments.body: A detailed viewer proposal reaches a result similar to the answer, though it follows a different line of reasoning. It begins with a British programme of 28-to-30-knot fast battleships that keeps shipyards working and signals commitment to the treaty. American naval planners might prefer a slower South Dakota-style ship because Congress could favour lower cost and greater protection over speed, while Japan has an incentive to wait, observe both programmes, and use its full allowance for a clean-sheet response with heavy firepower. The guns-armour-speed triangle is filtered through employment, legislative politics, industrial timing, and national strategy rather than tonnage alone.

evidence.note: He compares British, American, and Japanese design and procurement incentives.

segments.summary: Britain, the United States, and Japan would make different speed, protection, and construction choices under the same limits.
segments.question: What capital-ship programmes would Britain, the United States, and Japan pursue under the equitable treaty?
segments.answerShort: Britain would likely favour fast ships and steady construction, the United States might trade speed for cost and protection, and Japan would wait to tailor its response.

segments.title: Tiger as a fast specialist rather than a battle-line ship
segments.body: A highly modernized Tiger could be more useful than retaining older Queen Elizabeth-class ships in the battle line. Replacing early coal-and-oil machinery with later oil-fired small-tube boilers could test how much speed a reconstructed battlecruiser might gain. A 35-knot specialist would offer cruiser protection and deterrent value while generating practical knowledge for later designs. Slow non-treaty battleships, by contrast, would be outclassed outside the Atlantic and could become liabilities if asked to stand in a modern battle line.

evidence.note: He contrasts a modernized Tiger with older battle-line capital ships.

segments.summary: A rebuilt Tiger could retain value as a fast cruiser-hunter even while older battleships become liabilities.
segments.question: Would rebuilding Tiger be a better use of resources than retaining older British battleships?
segments.answerShort: Potentially. A very fast Tiger would have specialised utility, while old slow battleships would be dangerous to retain in a modern battle line.

segments.title: A proposal to balance cruiser limits and unfinished battleships
segments.body: A viewer proposes pairing a roughly 40,000-ton battleship ceiling with lower 15,000-to-18,000-ton heavy-cruiser limits. The idea is meant to satisfy peace factions while preserving meaningful design choices rather than eliminating them. The same comment argues that already-started South Dakota hulls might appeal to Congress because completion could be presented as avoiding the cost of scrapping work already done. The proposal remains contingent on the treaty's construction timetable, and the video offers no separate endorsement.

evidence.note: A viewer proposes lower cruiser limits and considers whether the construction timetable could preserve some already-started South Dakota ships.

segments.summary: A viewer proposes lower heavy-cruiser limits as a peace compromise while asking whether unfinished South Dakota hulls could survive cancellation.

segments.title: Why automatic escalation has a practical ceiling
segments.body: A proposal for predictable annual increases in displacement and gun calibre quickly reaches a practical ceiling. Starting from a 16-inch limit and adding a quarter inch each year reaches 18 inches in only eight years, while a 30,000-ton starting point rises to about 38,000 tons. Designers and governments would anticipate that endpoint rather than treating each annual step as an independent surprise. Once the system reaches the practical gun ceiling, continued automatic escalation offers little useful naval value.

evidence.note: He explains how scheduled escalation quickly reaches 18-inch guns.

segments.summary: A treaty that automatically increases tonnage and gun calibre would soon reach the practical limit of capital-ship weapons.
segments.question: Would a treaty with scheduled annual increases in ship size and gun calibre be more realistic?
segments.answerShort: It is an interesting idea, but it rapidly reaches the practical ceiling around 18-inch guns and very large displacements.

segments.title: Aircraft carrier limits are deferred to part two
segments.body: A viewer asks how the proposed treaty would assign total aircraft-carrier tonnage and cap the size of individual ships. The question also notes an understanding that effective carriers needed larger hulls. This installment does not settle either limit. It directs viewers to part two of the series, where the carrier provisions were addressed.

evidence.note: A viewer asks about total and individual carrier limits, and the answer redirects the question to part two of the series.

segments.summary: A question about carrier tonnage and individual ship size is redirected to the installment that covers aircraft carriers.
segments.question: How would the proposed treaty assign aircraft-carrier tonnage and limit the size of individual carriers?
segments.answerShort: This installment defers the detailed answer to part two of the series.

segments.title: Henderson also anticipated the aircraft carrier's rise
segments.body: A viewer suggests that no one besides Admiral Fisher could have foreseen the aircraft carrier's later importance. Henderson's career provides contrary evidence. Early British carrier advocacy therefore cannot be reduced to a single visionary figure. The brief reply does not develop Henderson's record in detail.

evidence.note: He rejects the claim that Fisher stood alone and identifies Henderson's career as counterevidence.

segments.summary: A brief correction places Reginald Henderson alongside John Fisher in anticipating the aircraft carrier's future importance.
segments.question: Was Admiral Fisher the only person who foresaw the aircraft carrier's importance?
segments.answerShort: No. Henderson's career is given as evidence that he anticipated it as well.

segments.title: Battlecruisers for trade protection and cruiser hunting
segments.body: Trade protection, interdiction, and cruiser hunting give Britain or Japan reasons to retain battlecruisers. Their speed could answer armed commerce raiders and threaten enemy cruisers while the main battle fleet handled heavily protected opponents. Only battlecruisers are expected to receive major modernization, mainly to preserve their speed relative to an emerging faster battle line. A continuing capital-ship programme would therefore make most pre-treaty battleships obsolete by the Second World War, with selective high-speed battlecruiser modernization the more plausible exception.

evidence.note: He discusses trade roles and the likely obsolescence of older capital ships.

segments.summary: Fast capital ships retain a role against commerce raiders and cruisers, but cannot substitute for the whole battle fleet.
segments.question: Would battlecruisers still have a role in a treaty system built around new capital ships?
segments.answerShort: Yes, especially for trade protection and cruiser hunting, but most old battle-line ships would soon be outclassed.

segments.title: Naval budgets, public spending, and warship exports
segments.body: A viewer questions how naval budget cuts affected the wider flow of money through the economy. The comment argues that government surpluses can restrain growth and tax receipts, while postwar Britain also faced a greatly weakened export market for warships. Continued capital-ship construction might, in this view, have sustained domestic industrial demand and encouraged overseas orders. The video gives no separate answer to this economic argument, so it remains a viewer's hypothesis rather than an endorsed account of interwar finance or export demand.

evidence.note: A viewer links naval budgets, government surpluses, the weak postwar export market, and the possibility that more capital-ship construction could attract overseas orders.

segments.summary: A viewer links naval budget cuts to public spending, industrial demand, and the collapse of Britain's postwar warship export market.

segments.title: Battlecruiser utility depends on relative speed
segments.body: A viewer suggests that battlecruisers retain a place while battle-line speeds stay below about 27 or 28 knots. Their role depends on creating a much larger speed margin, potentially through reconstruction to 35 knots or more. Early treaty battleships might make 28 or 29 knots, while later batches could become faster as the design evolves. Battlecruiser utility therefore depends on contemporary fleet speed rather than a permanent quality of the type.

evidence.note: A viewer links battlecruiser usefulness to battle-line speed, and Dr. Clarke explains how later treaty designs would erode the required speed margin.

segments.summary: A rebuilt battlecruiser needs a clear speed margin over contemporary battleships, and that margin shrinks as the battle line evolves.
segments.question: Could rebuilt battlecruisers retain a useful role as battle-line speeds increased?
segments.answerShort: Only with a clear speed margin, potentially around 35 knots, because successive treaty battleships would become faster.

segments.title: Trading speed and protection for a 16-inch battery
segments.body: A viewer applies the relationship among guns, armour, and speed to a treaty standard fixed at 16 inches. The proposal uses nine guns in triple turrets as its baseline, while twelve guns in quadruple turrets require protection or speed to be sacrificed and may push designers toward a shorter citadel. The same comment says that driving an existing battlecruiser to 35 knots would test waterline length, machinery power, propulsion efficiency, and cavitation. The reply calls such a reconstruction a tough ask, though it might be achievable.

evidence.note: He weighs nine versus twelve 16-inch guns and the difficulty of reaching 35 knots.

segments.summary: A viewer's 16-inch treaty standard pairs a nine-gun baseline with more demanding twelve-gun ships and 35-knot battlecruiser rebuilds.
segments.question: Could a 16-inch standard support twelve-gun ships or 35-knot rebuilt battlecruisers?
segments.answerShort: The viewer proposes nine guns as the baseline, while twelve guns or a 35-knot reconstruction would demand difficult compromises. The reply considers the speed increase possible but a tough ask.

segments.title: Simulation results expose the cost of design compromises
segments.body: The closing game action tests the consequences of earlier design choices inside the simulation. It is not evidence about a historical engagement. Superb remains in action after severe structural damage, while the rest of the British division leaves her isolated and pursues wounded opponents. Vengeance suffers heavily after the weight-saving downgrade to barbette protection, which is identified as a mistake when turret damage accumulates. Uneven ammunition expenditure and the survival of the all-forward ships connect protection trade-offs with the separate problem of controlling a force.

evidence.note: He reviews severe damage, ammunition states, division behaviour, and the consequences of reducing barbette protection.

segments.summary: The fictional battle turns earlier weight-saving choices into visible damage, ammunition, and force-control consequences.

segments.title: Two baselines for an equitable London treaty
segments.body: The closing preview says the London treaty installments will combine the two treaties because their failures belong to the same process. The second is described as a final attempt to preserve a system that adopted the opposite measures needed for survival. The counterfactual can start from the historical Washington settlement and try to correct it in London, or continue the equitable Washington framework already proposed. The choice remains open and is put to viewers rather than resolved in this episode.

evidence.note: He explains why the London treaties will be treated together and asks whether that counterfactual should begin from the historical or equitable Washington settlement.

segments.summary: The closing preview offers two starting points for the London treaties: the historical Washington settlement or the equitable alternative developed in this series.
